hints: Focus on the definition first, a chiral centre is a tetrahedral carbon with four different groups attached, so look for $sp^3$ carbons only.
Quickly cross out what cannot be chiral, all $CH_2$ groups, all $C=O$ carbons, the $C(CH_3)_2$ carbon and the ester side chain carbons.
Now check every ring junction and fused ring carbon carefully, as fused systems hide several stereocentres where three different ring fragments meet a hydrogen.
walkthrough:
**Recall the test for chirality**

A chiral centre is a carbon with four single bonds to four different groups.

Rule to use:
$$\text{chiral C} = C \text{ with 4 different single-bonded groups, no double bond, no two identical } CH_3 \text{ or H}$$

**Remove the easy non-chiral carbons**

This molecule looks scary, but most carbons are easy to reject. All $C=O$ carbons are planar, all $CH_2$ carbons have two H atoms, and the $C(CH_3)_2$ carbon on the left ring has two identical methyl groups.

The open ester side chain $-OCOCH_2CH(CH_3)_2$ also has no chiral centre because the $CH_2$ has two H atoms and the $CH$ has two identical $CH_3$ groups.

**Check the left and central six-membered rings**

Look at the junction between the left ring and the middle ring. The quaternary carbon with one methyl group is bonded to four different carbon fragments, so it is chiral.

In the middle six-membered ring, the carbon bearing the $-CH_2O-$ group and the carbon where the middle ring joins the left ring are both bonded to H plus three different ring or chain fragments, so both are chiral. That gives 3 so far.

**Count the fused 5-membered and 4-membered lactone part**

This is where students undercount. Every carbon at a ring fusion with one H is chiral because going left around the rings is different from going right.

There are four such carbons, the two carbons where the middle 6-ring fuses to the 5-ring, and the two carbons where the 5-ring fuses to the 4-membered cyclic ester. Adding these 4 to the previous 3 gives $3 + 4 = 7$ chiral centres in total.

options.A: 4 is too low. It typically counts only the most obvious centres such as the $-CH_2O-$ bearing carbon and one or two ring junctions, and misses the hidden stereocentres in the fused 5-membered and 4-membered lactone system.
options.B: 5 is too low. It usually comes from counting the central six-membered ring centres correctly but counting only one or two of the four chiral carbons in the fused cyclopentane plus beta-lactone fragment.
options.C: 6 is one short. This is the classic near miss where one fused ring junction carbon is thought to have two identical ring paths, when in fact the fused polycyclic framework makes all four paths different.
options.D: 7 is correct. After excluding $CH_2$, $C=O$, $C(CH_3)_2$ and the achiral ester side chain, there remain 7 tetrahedral carbons each with four different groups, 3 in the left and middle six-membered ring system and 4 in the fused 5-membered and 4-membered lactone system.
